headline: NASA diversifies. True Anomaly cashes in. Hypersonics still stalled.
deck: This week highlights shifts in procurement and funding in the space sector.

stories.head: NASA embraces European firms for data acquisition
stories.body: NASA has added three European companies to its Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition program, signaling a shift towards a more global approach in space data. This move comes as the agency seeks to diversify its sources, even if American firms still dominate the market. The inclusion of these firms underscores the growing recognition that space data is a multinational affair.
stories.soWhat: If you're a U.S. company in the space data game, it might be time to polish your international partnerships.

stories.head: True Anomaly secures $190M Series C funding
stories.body: True Anomaly has raised $190 million in its Series C funding round, bringing its valuation to $1.6 billion. This funding is aimed at enhancing its co-orbital security and space domain awareness capabilities, a timely focus as the U.S. Department of Defense continues to prioritize these areas. The infusion of cash suggests that investors are betting heavily on the need for advanced security in an increasingly crowded orbital environment.
stories.soWhat: In an era where cash is king, True Anomaly's success may just set the tone for future space security startups.

stories.head: Hypersonic glide vehicle tests continue to falter
stories.body: For the third consecutive quarter, hypersonic glide vehicle tests have slipped, raising concerns about the reliability of this technology. As defense contractors scramble to meet aggressive timelines, the repeated delays could indicate deeper issues in development and execution. This ongoing struggle to deliver on hypersonics might lead to a reassessment of priorities within military tech budgets.
stories.soWhat: If hypersonics are the future of warfare, we might need to recalibrate our timelines—again.

watchlist.title: Keep an eye on SpaceX's valuation
watchlist.body: With SpaceX's valuation reportedly hitting $470 billion, investors will be watching closely for any signs of movement in the secondary market.

watchlist.title: BAE's microchip passes tests
watchlist.body: BAE's new strategic defense microchip passing radiation tests could lead to increased contracts, but the real hurdle is actual deployment.

watchlist.title: Dual-use tech debate heats up
watchlist.body: The critique of 'dual-use' tech could influence future policy discussions, particularly around military applications and ethics.

watchlist.title: Palantir's TITAN extension implications
watchlist.body: Palantir's $480 million extension on the TITAN ground station program suggests a strong future for its government contracts, but also raises questions about competition.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.

tickers.note: Virgin Galactic's stock remains volatile as it navigates its path to commercial spaceflight.
Palantir's recent contract extension shows the company's stronghold in defense but raises questions about its long-term growth.
NASA's Space Launch System is still a topic of discussion as the agency looks to balance costs and timelines.
AST SpaceMobile's bull case is a reminder that even in aerospace, the numbers can tell a story of perilous balance.
